notes: ⚠️ THE 300 ms IS A TARGET, NOT A MEASUREMENT, and saying so is the point: DEC-0020 recorded this cost as explicitly unmeasured. A budget with no pinned environment, no timing boundary and no warm-up treatment produces a figure nobody can reproduce or dispute, and 'p95 under 300 ms' would have been satisfiable by measuring the wrong thing on an unstated machine. ⚠️ THE VERIFICATION CLAUSE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST, and it is not routine hygiene. Without it the easiest way to pass is to cache the compiled document — which would report excellent numbers while measuring nothing, and would ALSO violate DEC-0020's request-time requirement and AST-0030's finding underneath it. A void run is not a failure and must not be recorded as one; it means the instrument was wrong, which is a different problem from the budget being missed. ⚠️ The 300 ms is still a TARGET rather than a measurement, and DEC-0020's third obligation stands: if the first valid run misses it by a wide margin the answer is that decision's own second alternative, plain markdown for stage documents — not a larger number. ⚠️ EVALUATED 2026-08-28 (EVD-0071): FAIL, and the reason is not the compiler. Applying DEC-0020's second alternative would surrender the restricted-MDX contract to remove roughly 20 ms and would still miss the budget. That clause was written when the cost was unmeasured; it now is, and it is somewhere else. ⚠️ THE PROTOCOL ITSELF NEEDS ONE MORE PIN. It fixes the host, document, warm-up, sample and timing boundary, but 'no other significant load' is not enforceable, and the read is I/O and validation heavy enough that ambient load moves the p95 by 50%. A protocol whose verdict flips between identical runs cannot settle a pass/fail question, whatever the number is. ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-28: the 234-359 ms span was attributed here to reading all 253 artifacts per request. It is not. `readStageDocument` awaits `connection()` and reads the nine stage documents only — `lintProject` is not on its path. What inside that span costs the time is an open question, not a known cost. ⚠️ SUPERSEDED 2026-08-28 BY ACC-0037, WITH THE FAILURE LEFT STANDING. The outcome remains `fail` and this record remains readable: the budget was missed and that is history now, not a tick that was quietly flipped. What changed is the question being asked. This criterion bounded read-plus-compile, and the measurement showed the read dominates and the compiler does not, so ACC-0037 bounds the compile alone and QST-0025 carries the read as an open question. DEC-0025 records why the plain-Markdown fallback did not fire. ⚠️ THE SUCCESSOR IS NOT THIS ONE RELABELLED. Superseding a failed criterion with a wider version of the same claim would be editing the failure rather than answering it; the successor measures a different, narrower thing, and the part it dropped is carried by a question rather than dropped.
statement: The 95th-percentile server-side time to compile and render the largest stage document in the project is at or below 300 ms, measured under this protocol. ENVIRONMENT: the reference host, with its OS, Node version, Next.js version and CPU model recorded alongside the result; no other significant load. DOCUMENT: the largest stage document by byte count at the time of evaluation, named in the result. TIMING BOUNDARY: from the moment the request handler begins the planning-content read to the moment the rendered document markup is complete, measured server-side; network and client time are excluded. WARM-UP: 10 requests are issued and discarded before measurement begins. SAMPLE: the next 50 consecutive requests, issued one at a time with no concurrency, are the measured set. VERIFICATION: each of the 50 must be shown to have actually compiled — a counter incremented per compile, or an equivalent observation, reported with the result. A run in which any measured request did not compile is VOID, not a pass.
title: Per-request compilation stays within 300 ms at p95, under a pinned protocol

notes: 'Verified by observation, not by the absence of an error' is the tier-1 controller's own rule arriving here: a removal that reports success while the directory survives is retained, and the check has to be `exists()` rather than `!threw`. ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-08-29: THERE IS NO SECOND PROCESS, AND THERE NEVER WAS ONE TO OWN. This artifact previously said the launcher owns 'both the application process and the file watcher' and 'terminates the watcher with the application'. The watcher is chokidar, imported dynamically INSIDE the `next start` process and held by the change-stream service in that process's memory. A parent launcher cannot call `changeStream.close()` across that boundary without adding IPC or a shutdown endpoint, and neither is justified for a local-first tool. The old wording described a mechanism that could not be built, which is worse than an unmet obligation: it would have been 'satisfied' by a launcher that called nothing and reported success. ⚠️ WHAT IS TRUE INSTEAD, and all of it is enforceable. The launcher owns ONE child: the `next start` process. The change-stream service owns its watcher and closes it when its last subscriber leaves — already built and tested under TSK-0011. Terminating the application process releases any watcher still open through process teardown, which is the operating system's guarantee rather than the launcher's. `close()` stays what it is: a service and test lifecycle operation, never something the launcher claims to call across a process boundary. ⚠️ THIS CRITERION WAS UNSATISFIABLE AS WRITTEN, WHICH IS WHY IT IS AMENDED RATHER THAN REPHRASED. It required that 'no watcher process remains'. There is no watcher process, so the clause could never be observed either true or false — and an unobservable clause in a criterion whose whole point is 'verified by observation, not by the absence of an error' is the exact defect that rule exists to catch, sitting inside the rule. It is amended rather than superseded because it has never been evaluated: no measurement is being retired, and there is no failed outcome to preserve. ⚠️ THE HEARTBEAT PRECONDITION IS PART OF THE CRITERION, not of the test that runs it. The watcher is created lazily on first subscription, so a run that never subscribed would satisfy every remaining clause while having nothing to clean up.
statement: After the documented launch command is run and then terminated, the child process it started is gone, no process is listening on the application's port, and no temporary directory the launcher created survives — each verified by observation, not by the absence of an error. The run must have opened `/events` and observed a heartbeat before termination, so that a file watcher is known to have existed.
title: Stopping the launcher leaves nothing behind

notes: 'No further steps' is the testable half. DEC-0018 fixes the mode: `next build` then `next start`, never the development server. ⚠️ MARKED `pass` IN ERROR ON 2026-08-29 AND RETURNED TO `not-evaluated` THE SAME DAY. EVD-0073 recorded, in its own omissions, that the install branch was never taken: `node_modules` was present in every run, so the launcher printed `dependencies present; skipping install`. This criterion says 'on a machine with... no prior application state' and 'installs and starts'. Half of it was measured and the whole of it was ticked. ⚠️ THE EVIDENCE ITSELF SAID SO, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING. The omission was written down accurately and then contradicted by the outcome three lines later — a criterion marked against evidence that explicitly disclaims the thing being claimed. Recording an omission is not the same as honouring it. ⚠️ WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the documented command run in a disposable copy of the repository with no `node_modules` and no `.next`, installing, building, serving and cleaning up with no further steps. ⚠️ EVALUATED PROPERLY 2026-08-29 (EVD-0074) AND RETURNED TO `pass`. The documented command was run in a disposable copy holding only tracked files, with `node_modules` and `.next` confirmed absent. It installed, built, served and cleaned up in 27.2s with no further steps, and the install branch was asserted positively rather than inferred from the run succeeding.
statement: On a machine with the repository and Node present and no prior application state, the documented command installs and starts the application in production mode, and the project view responds, without further steps. The install is conditional and the command says which branch it took: a cold checkout installs; a warm checkout whose root lockfile is not newer than npm's installed-tree marker skips the install; and a missing or stale marker installs rather than guessing about a tree npm did not lay down. ⚠️ THE FRESHNESS COMPARISON IS AGAINST npm's MARKER, NOT THE `node_modules` DIRECTORY mtime. A directory's mtime moves only when an entry is added or removed at its top level, which reinstalling the same tree does not do, while `npm install` touches the lockfile every time — so comparing the two made the condition permanently true and the documented command reinstalled on every start, which is the outcome a conditional install exists to prevent.
title: The application installs and starts from one documented command

notes: ⚠️ WRITTEN FROM A MEASUREMENT, not from caution. AST-0039 recorded what production actually does when the compiler refuses a document inside a `<Suspense>` boundary: HTTP 200, because the shell has already streamed, and a React error digest with no message, no path and no position. The compiler's diagnostic is exact and reaches only the server log. ⚠️ 200 IS NOT THE DEFECT AND IS EXPLICITLY ACCEPTED. Streaming means the status is committed before the failure is known, and demanding a 5xx would mean giving up streaming for a document the operator can be told about in place. What is refused is INVISIBILITY — a blank region and a success status for a document the compiler rejected precisely. ⚠️ THE ESCAPING CLAUSE IS NOT HOUSEKEEPING. The diagnostic quotes the offending source, which is agent-authored content; rendering it as markup would let a refused document inject into the page that reports its refusal — turning the safety mechanism into the delivery route. ⚠️ 'The rest of the page still renders' is what makes this a criterion about ONE region rather than about error handling in general: the exit criteria live behind their own boundary and a refused document must not take them down with it.
statement: When the restricted compiler refuses a stage document, the served page renders an error inside the document region that (a) is visible in the response body, (b) names the document by a REPOSITORY-RELATIVE path, (c) carries a line and column, and (d) has its diagnostic text HTML-escaped rather than interpolated as markup. The stage's exit criteria and the rest of the page still render. A partial page returning HTTP 200 satisfies this criterion; a response whose document region contains only an opaque error digest, or nothing at all, FAILS it.
title: A refused stage document fails VISIBLY, in the document region, with a location

notes: PASS 2026-09-23 on EVD-0138, measured by killing real children rather than by making one throw. Inside the bootstrap, which runs before any journal exists: the project is byte-identical afterwards, no `.pi` survives, and an ordinary rerun completes. After the journal opens: what the killed run left records the phase in flight as running — true only because that status is written before the work — and carries an exact resume command naming the project. THE ARGUMENTS ARE PARSED OUT OF THAT COMMAND, not typed beside it, so a command naming another project, omitting `--resume`, or missing altogether fails the control; running them completes the remaining phases and leaves no journal. A failure in an agent phase leaves the scaffold and reports partial setup. THE MEASUREMENT FOUND FIVE DEFECTS IN THE LOCK, EACH FOUND BY THE CONTROL OR THE REVIEW OF THE FIX BEFORE IT, ALL NOW FIXED, AND ALL THE SAME MISTAKE: acting on a judgement about a file that can change, or that never proved what it was read for. A killed run's lockfile made every rerun wait out the two-minute stale window; clearing such a lock by read-then-unlink lets two recoveries both acquire; claiming it by rename moves a lock that went live in the meantime, leaving the name free for a waiter, which four racing recoveries caught in CI; reclaiming the gate introduced for that had the same shape again; and judging a gate abandoned by age treated a process stopped between creating its gate and writing its name into it as dead. Removing somebody else's lock is now serialised behind a gate beside it, taken by the recovery path and the waiter's stale break alike, with the judgement made inside it; reclaiming a gate is serialised by a token and happens only when the gate's record names a process on this host that is demonstrably gone; and nothing reclaims the token. Everything else fails closed: the command refuses with exit code 17 and names both files to remove. Setup still refuses another machine's lock, an unreadable one, and a live one.
statement: Killing setup after its journal has begun leaves a journal naming the last completed phase and an exact resume command; running that command completes the remaining phases. Killing it during the dependency bootstrap, which runs before any journal exists, leaves consumer project state unchanged, and rerunning setup repeats the locked install safely. A failure in any agent phase leaves an already-initialised planning scaffold in place and reports partial setup rather than rolling it back.
title: An interrupted setup resumes from its journal and never deletes valid content

notes: ⚠️ "EXACT UNMODIFIED" IS ENFORCED AS BYTES, AND THE CRITERION'S WORDING IS WHAT DECIDED THAT. Migration replaces bytes rather than appending them, so the question it answers is not "does this look like Kiln's block" but "is this, byte for byte, output nobody has touched". A trimmed comparison answers the first and reads as if it answered the second: an indented rule, a trailing space, a tab, a blank line inside the block or mixed line endings all compare equal, and the edit that is the evidence the block was not Kiln's to replace is what gets destroyed. ⚠️ THE MISSING-FINAL-NEWLINE CASE WAS SETTLED THE OTHER WAY ON PURPOSE. A legacy block whose trailing newline something stripped is short one byte Kiln wrote, so it is modified and is reported rather than migrated. The alternative was to amend this criterion to permit one normalisation, which buys an automatic migration in a rare case at the cost of the criterion no longer meaning what it says. The tolerance survives where it belongs — on an explicit rewrite, where the operator asked and the only duty is not to tidy anything unasked. ⚠️ "REQUIRES AN EXPLICIT CHOICE" IS ABOUT OWNERSHIP, NOT COVERAGE. An edited or malformed block can hold every rule Kiln would have written and still be somebody's own work, so the choice is required whether or not its contents happen to protect the paths. Deriving it from coverage produced a report offering two options and requiring neither. ⚠️ WHAT "NEVER SILENTLY REWRITTEN" TURNED OUT TO COVER, after four review rounds, is wider than a single check: consent is to replacing the bytes the operator was SHOWN, so an answer about one block does not authorise replacing a different one that replaced it, and a plan that reported operator-owned content writes nothing at all — not a create, not an append, not a migration — unless that exact file is still there and the answer was `rewrite`. Deleting the block one has just been told about is a plausible answer to being told about it; the run that recreated it for `keep` is the clearest statement of what this criterion forbids.
statement: A fresh project receives exactly one Kiln-marked block containing `.planning/`, `.pi/sessions/` and `.pi/runtime/`. An exact unmodified legacy block containing only `.planning/` is migrated to the extended block with every byte outside the markers preserved, and the migration is recorded and byte-stable on rerun. A block the operator removed or edited is reported and requires an explicit choice; it is never silently rewritten.
title: One owner writes the ignore block, and a removed block is not restored

statement: Merging Kiln's owned fields into a `.pi/settings.json` that carries third-party packages, unrelated keys and a custom key order preserves the value of every unrelated key and every unrelated package entry, and preserves the relative order of ordinary string keys. Integer-like property names follow the order Pi's and JavaScript's JSON parsing and serialization give them, not their original textual position. A file that is not valid JSON, whose root is not an object, or whose Kiln-owned fields hold invalid values is refused before anything is written, and the file is left byte-identical; unknown Pi and third-party fields are preserved rather than refused. Applying the same desired state again changes no bytes and does not change the file's modification time.
title: The settings merge preserves unrelated content, refuses invalid input, and is byte-stable

statement: The `.pi/settings.json` content produced by the settings merge and the `.pi/kiln.json` content produced by `ensureProjectId` contain no credential value, token, authorisation header or credential-derived fingerprint, and no absolute user path or `~` home reference, asserted over the bytes each produces.

A real Pi run over a trusted project discovers those package-owned resources, and the same run over an untrusted project discovers none of them - the control that makes the positive result mean something rather than describing what Pi would have done anyway.
title: The package declares what it owns, loads under trust, and is absent without it

statement: Each registered creation, mutation, activation and stage-attestation tool performs its write through the existing locked, atomic, validated implementation rather than reaching the filesystem itself, and every wrapper - read or write - resolves the content root through the shared resolver rather than deriving one. A wrapper adds only the Pi-facing schema and the rendering of a result: no validation rule, no id allocation, no trace rule and no write path is restated in it. Every result is structured, a refusal is returned as data rather than thrown as prose, and neither carries a credential, a credential-derived value or an absolute user path.
title: Every registered wrapper writes through the existing discipline and adds nothing to it

notes: ⚠️ SCOPED 2026-09-13 TO WHAT TSK-0046 PROMISES, AND NO FURTHER (O1, then F88). The criterion accepts the decision owner, the outputs and the exit criteria - the three things a canonical definition carries - together with the nine identities and their paths, byte determinism, the three drift classes by name, a check that writes nothing, and both CI platforms. A skill that printed it under Purpose would tell an agent what the stage is for on the strength of a field that never said so - the drift CMP-0033 exists to prevent, arrived at by relabelling rather than by duplication. ⚠️ MISSING AND ORPHANED ARE STALENESS TOO. A definition added without regenerating, and a definition removed while its skill stays packaged, are the same drift as an edited one; a check that only compared the files present on both sides would pass both. ⚠️ BYTE DETERMINISM IS WHAT MAKES THE CHECK MEAN ANYTHING. A generator whose output varies with line endings, key order or the clock makes every check stale on some platform, and a check that is always stale is one nobody reads.
statement: The generator produces exactly nine packaged stage skills, one per canonical stage definition - `kiln-stage-01-intake`, `kiln-stage-02-intent-decomposition`, `kiln-stage-03-discovery`, `kiln-stage-04-requirement-gaps`, `kiln-stage-05-solution-design`, `kiln-stage-06-risk-feasibility`, `kiln-stage-07-acceptance-criteria`, `kiln-stage-08-implementation-plan`, `kiln-stage-09-handoff` - each at `pi-package/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with that name in its frontmatter, and each carrying its definition's decision owner, its outputs - the typed artifacts, the outputs not yet typed and the output prose - and its exit criteria. The output prose is rendered as output prose and never relabelled as the stage's purpose. Generation is deterministic: the same definitions produce byte-identical files on every run and on every platform, with no timestamp and no machine-specific content. The check mode writes nothing, and fails naming each skill by name that is stale (its content differs from what the definitions generate), missing (a definition has no generated skill) or orphaned (a generated skill has no definition). The check runs in CI on Windows and on Ubuntu. The handwritten `kiln-planning` skill is neither adopted nor removed by generation or by the check.
title: Packaged skills are generated, and staleness fails a check

notes: ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-09-13 (F91, F92). The criterion said the override directory was registered after the packaged set, and it named three states. Pi 0.84.4 resolves project-settings skill paths ahead of package resources and keeps the first skill with each name, and TSK-0047 promises four states; the packaged-only state and the exact meaning of removal - the skill removed, the directory and the entry kept - are now stated, with one generated identity and path-based provenance. ⚠️ CONTROLS, RECORDED AS BEHAVIOUR (D9). An absent override directory is silently ignored: Pi skips a settings skill path that does not exist, emits no diagnostic, and the packaged skill loads. An untrusted project - no trust decision, or an explicit denial - loads neither the package's resources nor the override, because Pi empties project settings when the project is not trusted. Neither control is a Kiln refusal. ⚠️ R8, NOT CLAIMED. Kiln's settings merge keeps every existing project `skills` entry where it is and appends its own. Project-settings entries share Pi's precedence and keep their order, so an earlier project-settings skill path holding the same identity outranks Kiln's appended override entry. This criterion does not claim otherwise. ⚠️ R9 IS SETUP'S (TSK-0060). The entry is fixed relative to `.pi`; that it names the selected content root's `skills-overrides/` is for setup to guarantee. This criterion proves the entry in the default layout, where the content root is `<project>/planning-content`.
statement: In an isolated trusted project whose `.pi/settings.json` holds Kiln's package entry and the skill-override entry `../planning-content/skills-overrides` as produced by `mergeSettingsText`, the pinned Pi runtime's real resource loader, reloaded for each state, resolves the generated skill identity `kiln-stage-01-intake` exactly as follows. (1) Packaged only - the override directory exists and holds no skill: the loaded skill's `filePath` is the packaged `pi-package/skills/kiln-stage-01-intake/SKILL.md`, and Pi reports no collision for that identity. (2) Override present - `planning-content/skills-overrides/kiln-stage-01-intake/SKILL.md` declares that name: exactly one skill with that identity loads, its `filePath` is the override file, and Pi's collision diagnostic names the override file as the winner path and the packaged file as the loser path. (3) Override edited - the override's description is changed: the same override `filePath` loads, with the edited description. (4) Override skill removed while the override directory and the settings entry remain: the packaged `filePath` and the packaged description load again, and Pi reports no collision for that identity. In every state the other packaged skills still load from the package. Provenance is read from `filePath` and the collision diagnostic's winner and loser paths, never from model behaviour. Pi 0.84.4 resolves project-settings skill paths ahead of package resources, and the first skill loaded with a given identity wins, so this criterion claims only that the consumer override wins over the packaged skill, not over every earlier project-settings skill path.
title: A consumer override of a generated stage skill wins over the packaged skill, tracks edits, and reverts when removed

notes: Evidence split agreed 2026-09-18 during TSK-0049. This criterion stays a claim about model behaviour: the second question itself must differ, not merely the state it is derived from. title: The second question is chosen from updated state, not from a list

notes:
Amended 2026-09-18 under TSK-0050, before implementation, and again the same day (F18). The original statement named Stage 1 attestation alone. The boundary is the same act for artifact approval and for type activation and deactivation, so all three are stated here rather than left to the implementation to generalise. Material-change preview is a separate criterion, ACC-0115: that one is the orchestrator's behaviour before a mutation, where this one is the tool boundary that holds whatever the orchestrator does.

Authorisation is Pi's interactive confirmation channel, `ctx.ui.confirm`, called with the invocation's own signal and a 30,000 ms timeout. Only a literal `true` authorises the action. No UI context, rejection, cancellation, timeout, abort and an unexpected UI error all refuse and all write the bounded refusal record. They share one refusal code, `operator-confirmation-not-granted`, because Pi returns the same `false` for every one of them: with no UI bound `confirm` is `async () => false`, and in RPC mode a cancelled dialog and an expired timeout both resolve `false` through the same path, which is why the SDK's own timed-confirm example labels the result "Cancelled or timed out". A code claiming to separate them would be a distinction Kiln invented rather than observed. An unexpected UI error refuses without the raw error reaching the model or the record.

F18: what each operation DOES with Kiln's actor string differs, and this criterion claims only what is true of all three. All three receive `operator via Pi UI`. Attestation persists it as `decidedBy`, and activation persists it in the project manifest. Review status persists the `approved` status and returns the actor to the caller, but stores no approver: the artifact envelope in `schemas/common.schema.json` has no reviewer field. Adding one, or an approval history, is an artifact-schema and migration decision that TSK-0050 does not make, so neither this criterion nor the confirmation dialog claims durable attribution for an approval.

The refusal record is `state/operator-boundary-refusals.json`, bounded at the newest 100 entries and holding only validated identifiers and enums. Evidence is split: deterministic tests cover both the confirmed and the refused branch, including an injected UI context for the confirmed one, because a harness that answered the dialog would be acting as the operator. The retained RPC run leaves the dialog unanswered and shows refusal after the bound.
statement: An attempt by the orchestrator to attest or advance a stage exit criterion, to set an artifact's review status to `approved`, or to activate or deactivate an artifact type is refused unless the operator confirmed that exact action through Kiln's interactive confirmation channel during that same tool invocation. No model-supplied argument can carry an authorisation value or actor identity. After confirmation, Kiln supplies its own internal actor string to the underlying operation; any actor identity that operation records therefore comes from Kiln, not the model. The confirmation result does not outlive the invocation that obtained it. Where no confirmation channel is available, or the operator cancels, rejects, or does not answer, the tool refuses with a stable refusal code. On a refusal the target attestation file, artifact file and type manifest are unchanged in bytes and in modification time, and a bounded refusal record naming the operation, the refusal code and the target identifiers is persisted and reported by `kiln_project_status`.
title: The orchestrator cannot cross a user-owned gate

statement: Started in a consumer checkout, the orchestrator resolves the canonical sibling content root. In any state in which the tool's own bundled planning content would resolve instead - including `PLANNING_CONTENT_DIR` naming it, and a sibling that is a link into it - it refuses before authoring anything, and no file under either root changes. The refusal has two surfaces: the operator-facing refusal names both canonical absolute paths, the resolved content root and the tool root; the model-facing structured refusal carries a stable refusal code and stable placeholders for those paths, and no absolute path. Self-hosting is permitted only by an explicit, strict self-host marker that the launcher emits into the orchestrator's environment after it has validated `--self-host`; an absent marker, or any value other than the exact expected one, refuses.

statement: The endpoint returns exactly the keys service, protocol, runId, projectId and build — no more and no fewer, as a set rather than in a fixed order — with the service name and the versioned protocol fixed, the run and project identifiers equal to the ones supplied to this process, and the build version read from the package the running code was loaded from rather than from the environment, which could only ever match itself. A response carrying an additional key, missing a key, or carrying the two identifiers exchanged, fails; asserting only the absence of known sensitive patterns does not satisfy this, because it passes on every field nobody thought to pattern-match. Every field of a successful response is built from a validated value: both identifiers must be strings matching the fixed 32-character lowercase hexadecimal format, and the build version must match a character set containing no path separator, colon or whitespace. Nothing that fails those checks is echoed, so the absence of any absolute path, credential, session content or planning content holds by construction across the whole response rather than by scanning the output. An identity that is not whole is not an identity: a missing, unreadable or unsafe build version answers 503 exactly as a missing run identity does, never a 200 with a null field. Each failure answers with its own exact key set and a distinguishing error, never a 200 with fields missing and never an invented identifier. The status, headers and parsed body are observed over real HTTP for both the identified and the unidentified case, and the served identity is proved to come from the running process rather than the build by starting the application with an identity different from the one present when it was built.
title: The health response is exactly an identity, asserted field by field

statement: Two proofs are required together, because either alone passes in the arrangement this criterion forbids. Structurally: under the supervisor the application launcher is spawned with a private stdin the supervisor can WRITE to and CLOSE, while Pi is spawned with the terminal inherited. Behaviourally: with a launcher-side reader actively attempting to consume input, an exact sentinel written to the supervisor's own stdin is received by Pi and the launcher-side reader receives none of that sentinel — it is expected to receive the supervisor's later stop control message, which is its own channel working. A positive check that input reached Pi does not satisfy this on its own: it passes whenever Pi happens to win a read, including when both processes hold the terminal, which is precisely the defect. The control must fail when the launcher's stdin is changed from a private pipe to inherited terminal input, and a control that survives that mutation has not tested this criterion. The launcher continues to stop on the stop control message and on its stdin being closed. ⚠️ SCOPE OF THE EVIDENCE: the harness supplies a pipe rather than a pseudo-terminal, so what is proved is descriptor ownership and byte routing, not terminal line discipline or signal behaviour. The structural assertion is what ties it to the real topology — whatever descriptor 0 is, the launcher is not given it.
title: The background launcher cannot read the terminal, proved against an adversary

statement: With an unrelated server already answering on the chosen port, launch refuses rather than reporting the browser ready. A response carrying a wrong run identifier, a wrong project identifier, or arriving while the expected child is not alive, likewise fails readiness.
title: An unrelated healthy HTTP service does not satisfy readiness

statement: A port outside 1..65535 or a non-integer value is refused. When the default is occupied, interactive mode offers another available port for that invocation only and non-interactive mode refuses with an exact PORT recovery command. An automatically chosen port is never written into project configuration.
title: Port handling refuses out-of-range values and never silently persists a choice

statement: After Pi exits, after an interrupt, or after one Ctrl+C at the keyboard in an interactive Kiln session, both process trees are stopped within their grace periods, the port is free, and only files created by that invocation were removed. Seven things are observed and recorded SEPARATELY, because they fail separately and because any one of them standing for the others is how a shutdown claim becomes untestable. An observation that was not made is recorded as unmade and the shutdown is reported partial; it is never treated as one that passed. (1) Which of the three triggers ended the run — Pi exiting on its own, a signal, or the keyboard stop — each recorded where it was observed rather than supplied beside it, so the record cannot contradict itself. A signal is recorded where it was handled and never inferred from the processes having gone. The keyboard stop exists because an interactive Pi reads Ctrl+C as a key, so no signal occurs: Kiln's Pi extension consumes the key in the editor and in dialogs and writes a per-run notice before asking Pi to stop, and the stop is recorded as `keyboard` when the supervisor sees that notice, including when Pi's exit is observed first; it never records a signal that did not occur. A run ended by Pi exiting on its own records neither a signal nor a keyboard stop. (2) For each tree independently, either that it had already exited or that a stop was requested of it: a tree that was already gone is recorded as such and is not asked, and a supervisor that asks one tree and not the other looks identical to a correct one on every run where the unasked tree exits anyway. (3) That each tree's exit was independently observed, so one going never stands in for the other. (4) That where a graceful stop did not complete, escalation was bounded and its outcome observed — reported as unobserved rather than assumed when the process still did not go. (5) That the port accepts a fresh exclusive bind afterwards, observed by rebinding rather than derived from any process record: an exit code says the leader is gone and says nothing about a worker still listening. (6) That only runtime files this invocation created were removed, proved by a file it did not create still being present afterwards, not merely by its own being gone. (7) That the results are recorded independently for Windows and for the supported POSIX platform through CI, rather than one platform's pass standing for both, and that each platform's observation includes a KNOWN DESCENDANT of each tree rather than only the leader's exit code. The platforms differ in the only mechanism that matters here: a graceful signal is unavailable on Windows, and on POSIX a process group can be targeted only for a child spawned as a group leader — which the foreground agent cannot be, since a detached process cannot read the terminal, so its descendants must be enumerated and signalled individually. A descendant enumeration that fails is recorded as unmade, because an empty list would claim a tree with no children. On Windows both trees are held by jobs (the launch prerequisite below), so each tree's descendants are its job's members, listed and terminated through the job, and a job that cannot be listed is recorded as unmade in the same way. Two bounds are stated separately, because they cover different work and are paid at different times. THE WINDOWS LAUNCH PREREQUISITE: Pi and the launcher are each created suspended inside a job object held by a host process outside that job, with kill-on-job-close set, and each is resumed only once it is assigned, so every descendant, detached ones included, is a member of its tree's job from its first instruction. A host that cannot create the job, set its limits, create the process or assign it refuses the launch, and nothing falls back to a plain spawn or to process-table tracking. No Windows shutdown operation then reads a process table, so the process-table preflight is not run on Windows and is recorded as not run, with that reason. The hosts' start-up is the launch's own cost and is never counted against the shutdown budget. POSIX has neither job hosts nor a preflight. THE SHUTDOWN: from the trigger — Pi exiting, an interrupt arriving, or the keyboard stop's notice being seen, without waiting for Pi to exit — the whole teardown has one 8,000 ms deadline, and every operation draws its allowance from it: the descendant tracker joins, each tree's grace and hard waits, every identity read, every signal or `taskkill`, the launcher's control channel, the removal of this invocation's owned files, and the port probe. An operation whose minimum allowance the deadline cannot cover is not started, is named in the record's `unfinished` list with its reason, and makes the result incomplete. A shutdown is complete only when all six hold: both trees were observed stopped; the port accepts a fresh exclusive bind; the removal of owned files succeeded; every required observation was made, so `notObserved` is empty; `unfinished` is empty; and `withinBudget` is true. A teardown that ran past its deadline is not complete, whatever else it managed.
title: Shutdown leaves nothing running on either platform

A fabricated OAuth credential does not satisfy this criterion in any form.
title: OAuth is proved by a real login and its revocation, or it is not called verified

notes: PASS 2026-09-03, mechanised in `test/link-trace.test.mjs`. Each repair case asserts BOTH that the link is gone and that the lint finding it produced has cleared — `trace/wrong-target-type` for a wrong-type target, `trace/target-missing` for a deleted one, `lifecycle/trace-to-inactive` for a superseded one — because 'the array is shorter' was never the claim; 'the graph is repaired' is. Each fixture first asserts the finding EXISTS, so a case that stopped producing damage could not pass by repairing nothing. ⚠️ THE FIX IS AN ASYMMETRY AND BOTH HALVES ARE TESTED IN THE SAME FILE. Removal now inspects nothing about the target; addition still refuses a wrong type, a dangling reference and a malformed id. A later simplification that made them share one validation path would repair nothing and would pass a file that only tested removal. ⚠️ `answeredBy` OPENED FOR REMOVAL ONLY, and it is the only field that did. `supportedBy` and `refutedBy` still route to `unlinkEvidence` and `supersededBy` to `setLifecycle`, because those removal operations genuinely exist; `answeredBy` had none, which is what forced the deliberate exploitation of the companion defect during Phase 1. Adding an answer link still routes through `resolveQuestion`. ⚠️ THE WRITE DISCIPLINE IS ASSERTED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the fresh-read-inside-the-lock is proved by editing the file between the artifact's creation and the unlink and requiring the edit to survive; the atomic write by requiring no temporary file beside the artifact; and the lock by requiring it released. #16's amend-on-change is covered, including that a no-op does not amend.
statement: `unlinkTrace` removes a link whose target is of the wrong type, whose target does not exist, and whose target has been superseded — each verified by the link being gone and the lint finding it clears. It removes `answeredBy` entries, which no operation could previously withdraw. It continues to refuse an unknown FIELD, and it preserves the lock, fresh-read and atomic-write discipline. Adding a link is unaffected and still validates the target type.
title: An invalid or stale link can be removed through the typed path

notes: PASS 2026-09-03. The guard is now `Array.isArray(effectiveSchema(schemas, type).properties[k]['x-traceTarget'])`, asked PER TYPE rather than as a union, because a name that is a link on one type need not be one on another. It is the same source `linkTrace` validates against, so the two cannot drift. ⚠️ THE COUNT WAS EIGHT, NOT NINE, AND MY EARLIER ACCOUNTS OF THIS DEFECT SAID NINE. They included `implementedBy`, which is deliberately NOT a trace field — the component schema says so explicitly: 'Paths rather than a trace field on purpose: code is not an artifact, and pretending it is would put the repository inside the planning model.' It declares no `x-traceTarget`, the derived guard leaves it alone, and a test asserts that it stays revisable. Enumerating from the schemas is what surfaced the miscount; a hand-written list would have carried it. ⚠️ THE SCHEMAS DECLARE 25 TRACE FIELDS AND THE OLD LIST HELD 17. Every name in the old list was a real trace field, so the defect was never a wrong entry — it was the eight that were never added, which is the failure mode of any guard maintained by hand beside a declaration that already exists. `reviseArtifact` already resolved the effective schema a few lines later, for materiality, under a comment reading 'never from a hardcoded field list'. The rule was in the file; it just had not been applied to the guard above it.
statement: `reviseArtifact` refuses every field the schemas declare with `x-traceTarget`, established by enumerating those fields from the schema set at test time and asserting a refusal for each — not by comparing against a second list written in the test. Adding a trace field to a schema therefore extends the guard with no code change, proved by introducing one in a copied schema set and requiring the refusal. The eight fields that were previously reachable — `acceptedBy`, `answeredBy`, `blocks`, `evaluates`, `fulfils`, `raisedBy`, `satisfies` and `verifies` — are refused, while a non-trace field on the same type stays revisable so the guard is discriminating rather than simply refusing everything.
title: The trace-field guard is derived from the schemas, and covers every declared trace field

statement: Every file the transaction may write is resolved through its deepest existing ancestor and proved to lie beneath a root the caller explicitly authorised, and the same proof is repeated under the lock immediately before each write. A junction or symbolic link on a target's path refuses and nothing is written through it, including a probe, even when the path spells as one inside the project. A root the caller did not pass is not a root the transaction can write to, and the transaction lock is not a writable target. Each target's plan key is derived from its resolved path, so two entries that reach the same physical file refuse whether they differ only in spelling or arrive through two authorised roots that overlap, and one file merged under any of its spellings reaches the single entry planned for it.
title: Every write target is identified by resolution, not by spelling

statement: The write plan is built while this process demonstrably holds the transaction lock, and planning refuses when it is not held. A plan that refuses leaves the project as it was found, directories included: every probe file and every directory created in order to probe is removed on every exit path. Where a removal cannot be completed, the transaction refuses and names each path it left behind, retaining alongside it whatever refusal caused the attempt — a cleanup failure is never reported as success. Absence is confirmed by observing the path, not by trusting the removal call's error code.
title: Planning holds the lock, and a refused plan leaves the project unchanged

statement: When the content a merge would produce is byte-identical to what is already on disk, the transaction performs no write. The evidence is the file's modification time, not the merge's reported status.
title: A merge that would produce the current bytes writes nothing

statement: The journal is a planned, contained target validated against its schema before each write, and it records the whole ordered phase plan up front, marking a phase running before that phase's work begins. On failure it survives, naming the last completed phase and an exact recovery command, and nothing already written is rolled back. On success it is deleted, and a deletion that fails for any reason other than the file already being absent is reported rather than swallowed.
title: The journal is a planned target whose lifecycle is never silent

statement: Given a transaction that already holds the project lock, the initializer runs inside it and produces content byte-identical to a standalone run, with the marked ignore block appended at most once and every pre-existing line intact; a second run inside a held transaction still reports already-initialised and does not touch the ignore file. The transaction is accepted only as an authenticated, currently live capability: an object carrying the right shape but not issued by the transaction module is refused, a genuine transaction whose run has finished is refused, and one holding a different project is refused — each without writing anything. Work runs inside a transaction only by being registered with it, so a collaborator authenticated at entry is also enrolled for its duration rather than left to run beside it. A transaction is revoked before its lock is released and every operation through a revoked transaction is refused. In-flight work is drained to quiescence before revocation, including work started by work already being drained, so nothing registered with the transaction is still running when the lock is released. Where any work was still running at the moment the body returned, that work completes under the lock and the run is reported failed. No claim is made about operations the body did not await which had already settled: they are indistinguishable from awaited ones and cannot cross the release boundary. An acquisition of a lock already held further up the same call stack is refused immediately rather than waiting out its bounded retry, that refusal expires with the lock so an acquisition from an async context descended from a released lock succeeds, and two concurrent independent acquisitions in one process still serialise.
title: The initializer runs inside an authenticated, live transaction

statement: Started with a run identifier and a project identifier, the launcher validates both before use and the application it starts answers its health endpoint with exactly those values — observed from the application's response, not from the launcher's own output, since a launcher printing an identifier proves only that it parsed one. The port is parsed rather than coerced, and a value that is not a whole number between 1 and 65535 is refused before anything is installed or built; an empty value is refused rather than treated as unset, because a supervisor whose port computation produced nothing would otherwise bind the default and then poll the port it believed it had chosen. A partial, malformed or present-but-empty identity is refused with the offending variable named and its value not echoed, never treated as a standalone run: standalone means the variables are absent, not blank, and starting anyway would produce a shell the supervisor can never recognise, reported to the operator as a readiness timeout two processes away from its cause. The launcher stops on the stop control message arriving on the stdin it was given, and stops equally on that stdin being closed with no message — a supervisor that dies cannot send anything, but the operating system closes its pipes regardless. Both paths terminate the child, remove the run directory, and free the port. The application is given no stdin at all, so it cannot read from the handle the launcher's own control channel arrives on. Interactive standalone operation — a terminal on stdin, no identity supplied — is unchanged, and the existing content-root refusal, single-child ownership and cleanup behaviour continue to hold. Standalone operation on a PIPED stdin is deliberately not unchanged: closing that pipe stops the launcher whether or not a supervisor is present, which is the intended behaviour rather than a preserved one. This criterion makes no claim about readiness: the launcher propagates an identity, and confirming that the process answering is the one this invocation started is the supervisor's to establish.
title: The launcher propagates a validated identity and stops through the stdin it is given

statement: When Pi exits, the supervisor sends the stop control message on the launcher's stdin, requests that stdin be ended, and then waits for the launcher to exit within a bounded period, escalating if it does not. Three facts are recorded separately: that the message was sent, that the end was requested, and whether the exit was actually observed. A run whose launcher was never seen to exit is reported as a failure with the address something may still be listening on — not as a success carrying the agent's own exit code, since the agent finishing cleanly says nothing about whether the launcher went. Writing to the pipe never throws: a stream error is delivered asynchronously, so it is listened for rather than wrapped in a try. An error observed before the shutdown result is finalised is recorded on that result; one arriving after it is not, and the criterion claims no more than that — what proves the launcher went is the observed exit, not the error record. That the launcher REACTS to a stop message and to a close is established elsewhere and is not what this asks; what this asks is that the supervisor performs the contract, since a supervisor that never sends anything is indistinguishable from one that does whenever the launcher would have exited for its own reasons. The wait is bounded in both directions: returning before the child is gone leaves a process holding the port, and waiting without limit replaces a hung application with a hung terminal. ⚠️ SIGNAL HANDLING, BOTH PROCESS TREES, GRACE PERIODS ACROSS PLATFORMS AND INVOCATION-OWNED FILE CLEANUP ARE NOT THIS CRITERION'S. They are ACC-0081's, on TSK-0058; claiming them here would mark work accepted that nothing has built.
title: The supervisor performs the Pi-exit handoff and observes the launcher go

This criterion is re-evaluated once the supervisor sends /kiln-start on a new session only and a real-command control observes it. ⚠️ AMENDED 2026-09-24: the start prompt is required on a first INTERACTIVE run only. With piped input Pi runs in print mode and joins the piped text and a positional /kiln-start into one unexpanded message (EVD-0143), so a run whose input or output is not a terminal is sent no start prompt and its piped text is the first turn. Not re-evaluated until the four-cell CI run for the correction passes; EVD-0143 holds the local measurements. ⚠️ RE-EVALUATED 2026-09-24: PASS on EVD-0110 and EVD-0143. statement: A fresh start requires BOTH that no session record is present and that the session storage was successfully inspected and found absent or empty. Storage that could not be inspected — unreadable, or a regular file where the directory belongs — is not an empty one, and a record that exists but cannot be opened is not a missing one: only a genuine absence answers, and every other failure asks. Starting fresh over sessions nobody could enumerate is the failure this clause exists to prevent, and it is reachable by exactly those two routes. On a first interactive run, where Pi's input and output are both terminals, the supervisor sends the start prompt; on every first run it records the session it began. On a later run it resumes the exact session named in the record, proved by the session identifier the agent was invoked with matching the stored one — not by the agent having started successfully, which is equally true of a brand-new unrelated session and is the check this criterion exists to rule out. The record is accepted only when its project and its state mode both match the run: a state root can be shared or copied, so a record whose every field is individually valid can still belong to another project, and the mode decides which store the identifier refers to. When the record is missing, unreadable, invalid, foreign, recorded under a different mode, or names a session that is no longer there, the supervisor presents the sessions actually available and asks; it never silently resumes a different one and never silently starts a fresh one in place of a session the operator believes they are returning to. A non-interactive run refuses instead, with the exact recovery command for the shell it is running in. The record names a session and a mode and carries no absolute path, so a project moved or a state root relocated does not resume something belonging elsewhere.
title: A rerun resumes the exact recorded session, not merely a session

notes: ⚠️ AVAILABILITY AND `configured` DISAGREE, AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS MEASURED. The pinned runtime's `getProviderAuthStatus()` can report `configured: true` while `hasConfiguredAuth()` is false and the model is absent from `getAvailable()`; the compatibility spike's `withOAuth` cell records exactly that, with `statusDisagreesWithAvailability: true`. Anything gating on "some authentication source is configured" tells an operator they are connected when they cannot infer, which is why this criterion names the available-model set rather than the status object. ⚠️ THE PERMITTED CATEGORIES ARE THE THREE CMP-0029 DECLARES. Pi's own vocabulary is wider: `runtime` means a key was passed on the command line, and `models_json_command` and `fallback` are routes that produce a credential by executing something or by inheriting an extension's. None of the three is a category Kiln permits, so each is a refusal rather than a classification — mapping them onto `custom-environment-key` would let a route the table refuses arrive under a name it accepts. ⚠️ THE REPORT IS A CLOSED SHAPE, NOT A FILTERED ONE. Pi's `environment` status carries a `label` built from `getConfigValueEnvVarNames()` — variable NAMES — so a report assembled by spreading the status object leaks them by default. Asserting the absence of known-bad fields cannot see a field nobody thought of; asserting the exact key set can. ⚠️ WHAT THIS CANNOT REACH, and it is an evidence omission rather than a gap in the criterion: OAuth for a BUILT-IN provider needs an interactive `/login` against a real account. A `models.json` provider is composed with apiKey auth only, so a stored OAuth credential for one has no flow to resolve it — the spike records this as `oauthProvedForCustomProvider: false` and `oauthRemainsOpenForBuiltInProviders: true`. statement: Before a provider contract is accepted, a disposable restricted child using the pinned Pi SDK resolves the exact selected provider and model. Availability comes from that exact model appearing in the available-model set, never merely from the provider reporting configured. A successful report contains only provider, model, availability and an auth-source category permitted by the declared contract. Planted credentials, variable names, headers and credential-derived fingerprints appear in no report, refusal, stdout or stderr, against a positive control. All disposable state is confined to a temporary root removed on success and refusal.
title: The canary confirms the exact model is available and names a permitted auth source

notes: ⚠️ REOPENED 2026-09-14 (F114): NO RESEARCH OR VALIDATION RESULT OR REFUSAL REACHED THE MODEL. That criterion is about the write discipline of mutation wrappers - TSK-0044's work - and would have held TSK-0045 behind it while describing almost none of what TSK-0045 builds. ⚠️ A CAPABILITY CALL IS A READ, AND "CHANGES NOTHING" MEANS NO PERSISTED CHANGE. It mutates no planning content, no configuration and no stored state - no credential cached, no choice recorded, no file written. It does NOT mean the call touches nothing: `research_capability` makes a live request to the backend and `validation_capability` runs the interpreter, because #121 requires a capability to be PROVEN rather than declared, and #67 measured what a declared-but-unusable capability costs. A test asserting no request and no subprocess would contradict the rule the probes exist to satisfy; what must be asserted is that nothing persisted changed. ⚠️ DELEGATION IS NO LONGER HERE (F80, 2026-09-12). This criterion required each registered delegation tool to call "the existing implementation in `lib/`", and no delegation runtime exists there: it is CMP-0036's, built by TSK-0053 and TSK-0054, which TSK-0045 does not depend on. As written the criterion could not be satisfied by the task it accepts. `kiln_delegate` is now registered by TSK-0053 beside the runtime it builds, under its own criterion. ⚠️ THE FIVE WIRE NAMES ARE UNPREFIXED, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE (F79). `research_capability`, `research_search`, `research_fetch`, `validation_capability` and `validation_run` are the names `lib/specialists/contract.mjs` requires by key and `verifyChild` checks a child against; renaming them to `kiln_*` would break the contract and the child-signature check. ⚠️ THE SIGNATURE TOOL IS ACC-0109's, NOT THIS ONE'S. `kiln_capability` returning the package's declaration unchanged is accepted there; this covers the adapters beside it. ⚠️ THE PI WRAPPER IS THE DISCLOSURE BOUNDARY; THE VALIDATION CONTROLLER IS DELIBERATELY NOT (F84, 2026-09-12). Measured against the real lib/validation/: a validation_run result carries absolute machine paths by four routes - failure.message when provisioning fails (the interpreter and the vpw-tier1- workspace), destroy.retainedPath and the retained-workspace omission reason when cleanup leaves the workspace behind, and executions[].stderr or stdout when a job prints its own paths, as a Python traceback does. The controller keeps those precise paths on purpose, as diagnostics for its own callers, and is not changed. The Pi wrapper renders a sanitised COPY - the exact workspace root becomes <workspace> with its relative tail kept, the interpreter, temporary directory and home become <path>, and a general absolute-path scrub runs last - and leaves the controller object untouched. A separate controller issue is warranted only if another model-facing or persisted consumer shows a controller result without going through this boundary. ⚠️ CREDENTIAL BOUNDARY (D5). At handler invocation, the wrapper delegates without collecting credentials for redaction; the invoked research and validation implementations may read their own permitted environment inputs. The validation controller constructs the allowlisted child environment, and tests prove a planted credential reaches neither the controller result nor the rendered result.
statement: Each registered research and validation tool performs its work by calling the existing implementation in `lib/` rather than restating its rules: no capability decision, retrieval policy or validation rule is re-implemented in the wrapper. A capability call reports what is available and changes nothing - no planning content, no configuration and no stored state. Every result and every refusal is structured data, and neither carries a credential, a credential-derived value or an absolute user path.
title: The research, validation and delegation adapters call the implementations that already exist

notes: ⚠️ REGISTRATION MOVED HERE FROM TSK-0045 (F80, 2026-09-12). TSK-0045 promised to register a delegation adapter over an implementation that does not exist: the delegation runtime is CMP-0036's, TSK-0045 depends only on TSK-0043, and its criterion required each adapter to call "the existing implementation in `lib/`". The registration now sits with the runtime it wraps. ⚠️ WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER. Whether the runtime's own rules hold is ACC-0076's; whether a child without the Kiln capability signature is refused is ACC-0075's. This covers only the boundary between Pi and that runtime - which is why it evaluates CMP-0032 rather than CMP-0036.
statement: The registered `kiln_delegate` tool performs a delegation by calling the delegation runtime it is registered beside, and restates none of that runtime's rules: not the child's launch arguments, not the task binding, not model or thinking-level inheritance, not the intersected tool allowlist, not the timeout, not the abort propagated to the process tree, and not the cleanup of temporary material. The wrapper adds only the Pi-facing schema and the rendering of a result. Every result and every refusal is structured data returned to the caller rather than thrown as prose, and neither carries a credential, a credential-derived value or an absolute user path.
title: The delegation tool adds a schema and a rendering, and no rule of its own

notes: ⚠️ DEFERRED FROM TSK-0046 ON PURPOSE (O1 and F88, 2026-09-13). TSK-0046 promised these seven, and no canonical definition carries any of them: `stages/*.json` has a name, a decision owner, outputs and exit criteria, and nothing else. A generator asked to emit them would have to write them into its own templates or borrow another field, which recreates exactly the drift CMP-0033 exists to prevent - two descriptions of one pipeline, each invisible from the other. So the definitions gain the fields first, and generation follows. ⚠️ PURPOSE WAS NEARLY BORROWED (F88). The first generator printed `producesProse` under Purpose. That field describes outputs; relabelling it is inference by another route, and it is refused for the same reason a template default is. ⚠️ A TEMPLATE DEFAULT IS A FAILURE, NOT A CONVENIENCE. A skill that says 'delegate as appropriate' because its definition was silent reads exactly like one whose definition said so; refusing the definition is the only way the gap stays visible. ⚠️ THE SPLIT, STATED EXACTLY (corrected 2026-09-20, D50-D56). The earlier wording said delegations and the mutation boundary both "name roles, not rules", which is true of one and misleading about the other. Three separate authorities apply. (1) DELEGATION ROLES AND CAPABILITIES ARE CHECKED AGAINST THE SPECIALIST CONTRACTS. A delegation declares `role` and `capabilities` independently; the loader validates the role against `ROLES` and requires the declared capabilities to equal `contractFor(role).requiredCapabilities`, sorted and unique. It never derives or replaces them, so a definition and a contract that disagree are a refusal rather than a silent rewrite. A role whose contract requires nothing declares `"capabilities": []` explicitly, and a stage that delegates nowhere declares `"delegations": []`. (2) CREATION AUTHORITY REMAINS `produces`, AND THE MUTATION BOUNDARY DOES NOT RESTATE IT. `stages/` already defines what a stage produces and `lib/stages.mjs` opens by warning that two hand-maintained descriptions of one pipeline disagree. A `mayCreate` list would be that second description, so there is none. (3) `mutationBoundary` NAMES CANONICAL NON-CREATION OPERATIONS. Its `mayMutate` entries are operation identifiers - the registry mutation keys plus `writeStageDocument`, `writeStageAttestation` and `setTypeActivation` - not artifact types and not tool wire names. It therefore says what a stage may CHANGE, while `produces` says what it may CREATE, and neither can be read as a weaker copy of the other. This still depends on TSK-0051, because the roster and the contracts it settled are what (1) is checked against.
statement: Each canonical stage definition in `stages/*.json` declares its purpose, its method, its rules for selecting the next question or activity, its allowed delegations with the capabilities each requires, its mutation boundary, its approval boundary and its expected completion summary, and each generated `kiln-stage-<stage-id>` skill carries those seven from its definition. None of them is supplied by the generator's templates or inferred from another field - in particular a stage's purpose is not taken from `producesProse`, which describes its outputs. The generator refuses a definition that lacks a required field rather than filling it in, and the check fails, naming the skill, when any generated field no longer matches its definition.
title: Every stage skill carries its purpose, method, next activity, delegations and boundaries from the canonical definition

The turn is retained as recorded output, and its judgement - one question, no solution - is made by a human reviewer against that record, not by the model and not by a scripted provider.
title: In the clean-consumer journey, the first Stage 1 turn asks one question and proposes no solution

notes:

This is a single orchestrator-wide behaviour stated once, not TSK-0071's per-stage mutation policy: TSK-0071 owns a per-stage mutation-boundary field, and this criterion declares no stage-definition field. statement: Before calling a tool that creates or mutates a typed artifact, the orchestrator states in a separate turn which artifact it proposes to create or change and what the change would be, and waits for the operator. If the operator rejects the proposal, cancels, or does not reply, no mutating tool call is made. Capturing an operator's own answer into a stage document is excluded, because that records the operator's reply rather than proposing a change to the project. Approval, activation and attestation are governed by ACC-0070 rather than by this criterion.
title: The orchestrator states a material change before making it
